outline.section: H2: Why Your Hair Gets Dry (and What Actually Fixes It)
outline.guidance: Briefly explain the biology of dry hair: the cuticle layer lifts when hair is damaged or dehydrated, causing moisture loss, frizz, and breakage. Introduce the concept of hair porosity — low, medium, and high — because porosity determines how well ingredients penetrate and which DIY masks will work. Mention that high porosity hair loses moisture fastest and needs heavier occlusive ingredients (like shea butter or coconut oil), while fine or low porosity hair can be weighed down by heavy oils. Keep this section educational and jargon-light. Do not recommend any specific products here — this section is purely 'why' before the 'how.' Cite a credible source (e.g., a peer-reviewed journal or a Healthline/PubMed-backed article) on cuticle structure or hair porosity.

outline.section: H2: The Best Natural Ingredients for a DIY Hair Mask
outline.guidance: Cover the top 6-8 natural ingredients used across the most effective DIY hair mask recipes. For each ingredient, give: (1) what it does, (2) the science behind it (brief, one to two sentences), and (3) which hair type it suits best. Required ingredients to cover: coconut oil (lauric acid penetrates hair shaft — cite a peer-reviewed study, e.g., Rele & Mohile, 2003, Journal of Cosmetic Science), honey (humectant, draws moisture from environment), avocado (fatty acids, vitamins E and B), banana (silica for strength, reduces breakage), shea butter (emollient, seals moisture especially for 4a and 4b hair types), olive oil (good for thick or high porosity hair), egg (protein for damaged or over-processed hair). Include a NOTE for fine hair: heavy oils like coconut oil can weigh down fine strands — use sparingly or choose lighter alternatives. This section is a key differentiator — go deeper than competitors who just list ingredients without explanation.

outline.section: H2: 5 Best DIY Natural Hair Masks for Dry Hair (By Hair Type)
outline.guidance: Present 5 curated recipes organized by hair type or concern — not just a generic numbered list. This is the core of the article. Each recipe should include: a clear subheading (H3), a one-sentence 'best for' callout, a short ingredient list with measurements, step-by-step instructions, how long to leave on, and one tip or common mistake to avoid. Recipes to include: (1) Coconut Oil + Honey Mask — best for normal to thick dry hair; note the lauric acid penetration benefit and link to the internal coconut oil blog post; (2) Avocado + Olive Oil Mask — best for high porosity or color-treated dry hair; (3) Banana + Shea Butter Mask — best for 4a/4b coily hair needing deep moisture; stress the importance of blending banana completely to avoid residue; (4) Egg + Honey Protein Mask — best for dry, damaged, or over-processed hair; caution: do not use in very hot water or egg will cook; (5) Plain Greek Yogurt + Olive Oil Mask — best for fine wavy or dry wavy hair needing lightweight hydration without buildup. For each recipe, include a 'make it better' micro-tip (e.g., apply heat with a shower cap to boost penetration). Keep instructions scannable using numbered steps.

outline.section: H3: Avocado + Olive Oil Deep Moisture Mask
outline.guidance: Best for: high porosity, color-treated, or chronically dry hair. Ingredients: half a ripe avocado, 1 tbsp olive oil, optional 1 tsp honey. Instructions in numbered steps. Note that avocado's oleic acid helps penetrate the cuticle while olive oil seals the outer layer. Tip: add a drop of essential oil (lavender or peppermint) for scalp stimulation.

outline.section: H3: Banana + Shea Butter Moisture Seal Mask
outline.guidance: Best for: 4a and 4b coily hair types that need heavy moisture retention. Ingredients: 1 ripe banana, 2 tbsp shea butter (softened), 1 tsp coconut oil. Instructions in numbered steps. CRITICAL TIP: blend the banana in a blender until completely smooth — lumps are nearly impossible to rinse out of tightly coiled hair. Explain that shea butter forms an occlusive layer that locks in moisture especially on high porosity strands.

outline.section: H3: Egg + Honey Protein Repair Mask
outline.guidance: Best for: dry, brittle, or chemically processed hair needing protein. Ingredients: 1 whole egg, 1 tbsp honey, 1 tsp olive oil. Instructions in numbered steps. Important warning: always rinse with cool or lukewarm water — hot water will cook the egg in your hair. Note that eggs should not be used more than once a week on hair that is not protein-deficient, as protein overload can cause brittleness.

outline.section: H2: How to Apply a DIY Hair Mask for Best Results
outline.guidance: This is a key differentiator — most competitor posts skip proper application technique. Cover: (1) Start on clean, damp hair — explain why (open cuticle absorbs ingredients better); (2) Section hair and apply from mid-lengths to ends first, then roots if scalp is dry; (3) Use a shower cap or wrap with a warm towel to trap heat and boost penetration; (4) Leave on for 20–30 minutes (not overnight for protein masks — risk of overload); (5) Rinse thoroughly with cool water; (6) Follow with a gentle shampoo only if needed. Also briefly mention that a good routine pairs the mask with a complementary leave-in conditioner for lasting hydration and, when heat styling, a heat protectant. Use this as a natural opportunity to mention that going beyond the mask — choosing clean daily hair care products — reinforces the results.

outline.section: H2: How Often Should You Use a DIY Hair Mask?
outline.guidance: Short, practical section. General guidance: once a week for very dry or damaged hair; every two weeks for moderately dry hair; once a month for maintenance. Note that protein masks (egg-based) should not exceed once a week and less often for low-porosity hair. Briefly explain that over-masking can lead to buildup or protein overload. Keep this section tight and scannable — use a simple frequency table or bullet list rather than dense paragraphs.
